title: Axial Flow Pump

introduction.definition: An axial flow (propeller) pump moves liquid parallel to the shaft: propeller blades act like a ship's propeller, adding swirl and pressure, and guide vanes downstream remove the swirl. It delivers very large flows at low head and has the highest specific speed of rotodynamic pumps.
key_points: Steep head curve; power highest at shut-off — never start against a closed valve
Some designs have adjustable blade pitch

classification.configuration: Vertical wet pit, single stage, line-shaft

introduction.summary: A propeller pump adds energy almost entirely by the lift of its blades, like a ship propeller working in a tube: liquid passes straight through axially. Straightening vanes above the propeller remove the swirl and recover pressure. It delivers very large flows at low heads with high specific speed; the head–flow curve is steep and power rises toward shut-off, so these pumps must not be started or run against a closed valve.

steps.text: Water enters through the suction bell.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Very steep head curve with a stall dip at part load; power rises towards shut-off (maximum at zero flow).

parts.name: Discharge Elbow Head & Floor Plate
parts.function: Turns the flow from the vertical column into the horizontal discharge pipe, supports the pump from the floor and carries the motor.
parts.material: Carbon steel, stainless; coated internally for seawater.

parts.name: Stuffing Box Packing & Gland
parts.function: Seals the shaft where it leaves the discharge elbow.

parts.name: Motor Stand
parts.function: Supports the vertical motor and gives access to coupling and gland.

parts.name: Adjustable Spacer Coupling
parts.function: Transmits torque and axial thrust to the motor thrust bearing; nut sets impeller/propeller axial position.

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Frame & End Shields
parts.function: Encloses the stator and supports the bearings; feet or flange mount the motor to the baseplate or pump.
parts.material: Cast iron or aluminium frame; steel fasteners.

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Stator
parts.function: Produces the rotating magnetic field.
parts.material: Silicon electrical steel, copper magnet wire, Class F/H insulation (typical).

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Rotor & Shaft
parts.function: Converts the rotating field into shaft torque (squirrel-cage induction rotor).
parts.material: Electrical steel, die-cast aluminium or copper.

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Bearings (DE & NDE)
parts.function: Support the motor rotor at drive and non-drive ends.

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Cooling Fan
parts.function: Draws cooling air over the finned frame.

parts.name: Vertical Motor – Fan Cover
parts.function: Guards the fan and directs air along the fins.

parts.name: Column Pipe – Upper
parts.function: Carries liquid from the bowls to the head and suspends the bowl assembly.

parts.name: Column Pipe – Lower
parts.function: Carries liquid from the bowls to the head and suspends the bowl assembly.

parts.name: Bearing Retainer (Spider) 1
parts.function: Holds the line-shaft bearing concentric at each column joint.

parts.name: Line-Shaft Bearing 1
parts.function: Supports the line shaft radially between head and bowls.

parts.name: Diffuser Bowl (Straightening Vanes)
parts.function: Removes swirl from the propeller discharge and converts velocity into pressure before the column.

parts.name: Diffuser Hub Bearing
parts.function: Radial support of the pump shaft in each bowl, the discharge case and the suction bell.

parts.name: Propeller Housing (Liner)
parts.function: Close-fitting liner around the propeller blade tips.

parts.name: Propeller (4-Blade)
parts.function: Adds energy to the liquid by blade lift, accelerating flow axially.

parts.name: Suction Bell
parts.function: Guides liquid smoothly into the first-stage impeller and holds the bottom bearing.

parts.name: Suction Bell Bearing
parts.function: Radial support of the pump shaft in each bowl, the discharge case and the suction bell.

parts.name: Pump & Line Shaft
parts.function: Transmits torque from the driver to the bowl shaft.

foundation: Motor stand / discharge head on a rigid floor; bell located per ANSI/HI 9.8 sump geometry.
alignment: Plumb column and motor coupling alignment.
piping: No discharge valve that can be closed during start, or start with it open; use flap valves/siphon breakers on outfalls.
commissioning: Check submergence and vortex-free approach flow.

overhaul.task: Inspect blades for cavitation and erosion.

lubrication: Water- or grease-lubricated column bearings per design.

remedies: Operate on the stable part of the curve

video_tutorials.title: Axial Flow Pump — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Axial Flow Pump.
An axial flow (propeller) pump moves liquid parallel to the shaft: propeller blades act like a ship's propeller, adding swirl and pressure, and guide vanes downstream remove the swirl.
It delivers very large flows at low head and has the highest specific speed of rotodynamic pumps.
Typical applications include flood control and storm-water stations; power-plant condenser cooling water; irrigation and drainage; evaporator and crystalliser circulation (alumina, chemical).
The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Diffuser Bowl (Straightening Vanes), Propeller Housing (Liner), Propeller (4-Blade), Suction Bell.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

script.narration: How the Axial Flow Pump works.
Water enters through the suction bell.
The rotating propeller blades lift the water axially and add swirl.
The diffuser guide vanes remove swirl and recover pressure.
The column and discharge elbow lead the flow out.

video_tutorials.title: Axial Flow Pump — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Axial Flow Pump.
Check vibration and bearing temperature.
Inspect propeller tip clearance.
Inspect blades for cavitation and erosion.
Watch for operation in stall zone: noise, vibration, power surge. Common cause: throttled or high system head.
Watch for cavitation: blade pitting. Common cause: low submergence.
Watch for overload on start: motor trips. Common cause: starting against a closed valve.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
